lead: Wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) sends several light signals through one fiber at the same time, each on its own wavelength. One laser and its modulator give only a few Gb/s, while the 1550 nm window holds tens of THz. WDM uses that window as many separate channels, so capacity grows with the number of channels N, not with electronic speed. Telephone backbones, cable TV feeds and data-centre links use it.
prereq: You need Unit 1 (single-mode fiber, V-number) and Unit 3 (laser sources, external modulators).

sections.h3: Why one fiber carries many colours

blocks.text: WDM assigns each signal a different wavelength λ, called a channel. All channels share one fiber. If there are N channels and each carries B bit/s, total capacity is C = N × B, as long as the fiber passband and the receivers allow it. This is the main reason WDM exists: one laser and modulator give a few Gb/s, but the 1550 nm window spans tens of THz.

blocks.where: C is total bit rate in bit/s; N is the number of wavelength channels; B is the bit rate per channel in bit/s.
Δλ is channel spacing in wavelength (m); λ is the operating wavelength (m); Δf is channel spacing in frequency (Hz); c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light in vacuum.

blocks.text: At 1550 nm, a 100 GHz slot is about 0.8 nm. The same 100 GHz slot is wider in nanometres at longer wavelengths because Δλ grows as λ². ITU-T grids put channels on exact frequencies near 193.1 THz. 100 GHz spacing is common; 50 GHz doubles the channel count in the same band. DWDM uses tight spacing, often 50 or 100 GHz, with temperature-controlled lasers. CWDM uses 20 nm spacing from 1270 nm to 1610 nm, uncooled lasers and short reach.

A multiplexer combines λ<sub>1</sub>…λ<sub>N</sub> into one fiber; a demultiplexer separates them. Some syllabi say “wavelength multiplexer” or “WDM mux/demux” for the same pair. Five common parts do this job.

items: Prism: refraction angle changes with wavelength; simple, low channel count.
Diffraction grating: periodic grooves send each wavelength to a different angle; good for many channels.
Thin-film dielectric filter: a stack of layers passes some wavelengths and reflects others; used in mux/demux and add/drop.
Arrayed waveguide grating (AWG): waveguides with fixed path differences interfere so each wavelength focuses on a different output; common in integrated optics.
Fiber Bragg grating (FBG): a periodic index pattern in the fiber reflects one wavelength and passes the rest.

blocks.text: Four parameters describe a mux or demux. Insertion loss is the drop in dB from input to wanted output; lower is better. Adjacent-channel crosstalk is the leakage power from the next channel divided by the wanted channel power, in dB; the leakage is smaller, so the value is negative and more negative is better. Channel uniformity is the spread in dB between the strongest and weakest output. Passband width is the range of wavelengths over which loss stays low. Coupler and grating physics is in 6.2.

The comb is the set of channel frequencies. Its width is roughly (N − 1)Δf, not NΔf, because N channels have N − 1 gaps. Capacity grows with N, but N is limited by amplifier gain band (see 6.3), laser wavelength drift, filter passband and crosstalk. A mux with 1.5 dB insertion loss removes 1.5 dB from every channel; a demux adds more. Passband width must cover laser drift and modulation chirp. Adjacent-channel crosstalk sets how close channels can be. In a network, each channel becomes a lightpath, see 6.5.

examples.question: A DWDM system uses 40 channels on the ITU grid near 1550 nm, spaced 100 GHz apart, each carrying 10 Gb/s. (a) Find the total capacity. (b) Find the spacing in nanometres using Δλ = λ²Δf/c. (c) Find the width of the whole comb. (d) In a 3.2 THz band with 100 GHz spacing, how many 10 Gb/s channels fit?
steps: Step 1: N = 40 channels and B = 10 Gb/s per channel. Total capacity C = N × B = 40 × 10 = 400 Gb/s.
Step 4: N channels have N − 1 = 39 gaps. Comb width = 39 × 0.8008 = 31.2 nm.
Step 5: Band = 3.2 THz = 3.2 × 10¹² Hz. Number of channels = 3.2 × 10¹² ÷ (100 × 10⁹) = 32. Capacity = 32 × 10 = 320 Gb/s.
examples.answer: The answers are 400 Gb/s total capacity, 0.8008 nm spacing, 31.2 nm comb width, 32 channels and 320 Gb/s in the 3.2 THz band.

traps: 100 GHz is not always 0.8 nm: Δλ = λ²Δf/c, so the same frequency spacing is wider at 1600 nm than at 1300 nm.
Total capacity is N × B per direction; multiply by 2 for a duplex pair only if the question says both directions are counted, and never multiply by N a second time.
CWDM is 20 nm spacing over 1270–1610 nm; DWDM is tight 50/100 GHz spacing. Do not mix the names.
Crosstalk is given as a negative dB ratio; −30 dB is better than −20 dB. Insertion loss is positive dB.
Mux and demux are named from the direction of the wanted signal; a passive part can often work either way.

quiz.a: A wavelength that carries its own independent data signal through the shared fiber.

quiz.q: State the ITU-T reference frequency near 1550 nm and two common channel spacings.
quiz.a: Reference frequency 193.1 THz; common spacings 100 GHz and 50 GHz.

quiz.q: Why does WDM raise capacity without faster electronics?
quiz.a: It adds parallel wavelength channels, each running at the electronic bit rate B, so total capacity is N × B.

quiz.q: A link has 32 WDM channels, each at 10 Gb/s. Find the total capacity.
Find Δλ for 50 GHz spacing at 1550 nm.
A mux has −25 dB adjacent-channel crosstalk and 1.5 dB insertion loss. What do these mean?
quiz.a: Insertion loss removes 1.5 dB from the wanted channel. Crosstalk leakage is 25 dB below the wanted channel; more negative crosstalk is better.

quiz.q: Why can the same 100 GHz grid not be described as a fixed 0.8 nm across 1270–1610 nm?
quiz.a: Because Δλ = λ²Δf/c, so the wavelength spacing changes with λ². It is about 0.8 nm at 1550 nm but different at 1270 nm or 1610 nm.

quiz.q: Give one practical difference between CWDM and DWDM.
quiz.a: CWDM uses 20 nm spacing, uncooled lasers and short reach; DWDM uses tight 50/100 GHz spacing, temperature control and long reach.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems use flexible-grid ROADMs, coherent 400G/800G channels and L-band extension. Research moves to space-division multiplexing, where multiple cores or modes share a fiber. Search terms: ITU-T G.694.1, CWDM grid, AWG, ROADM, flex grid.
